TEM/SAED for amorphous versus crystalline phase identification
Surface chemical analysis (XPS) to evaluate surfactant incorporation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surfactant-added samples do not show a significant delay in crystallization or exhibit degraded amorphous quality (or contamination-induced issues), the hypothesis is falsified.

hypotheses.builds_on: The rapid electrodeposition process that produces amorphous structures and the known ability of surface modifiers to influence nucleation kinetics.
hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes using an organic surfactant tailored to interact with phosphorus on the depositing nanoparticles—a strategy not employed in the original paper—to kinetically trap the amorphous state and improve thermal stability.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Slightly increasing the phosphorus content beyond near-equimolar ratios in the high-entropy alloy will enhance glass-forming ability and thermal stability by promoting a more interconnected, network-forming structure.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A baseline phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy synthesized via nanodroplet-mediated electrodeposition with near-equimolar elemental ratios.
hypotheses.intervention: Adjust the precursor solution ratios so that the phosphorus concentration is increased by about 5–10% relative to the other constituent metals.
hypotheses.conditions: Effective when the overall high mixing entropy is maintained; the increase in phosphorus must not lead to phase separation or excessive formation of P-rich crystalline domains.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: An increased concentration of phosphorus enhances the covalent or directional bonding interactions that build a more rigid and interconnected amorphous network.
hypotheses.mechanism: Phosphorus, when present as a network former (as in phosphosilicate glasses), can increase the number of topological constraints in the structure. This extra connectivity reduces atomic mobility during cooling, thus resisting the nucleation and growth of crystalline phases and raising the onset temperature for crystallization.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy should exhibit a higher thermal stability of the amorphous state—with an increased crystallization onset temperature—and improved glass-forming ability compared to the equimolar baseline.
hypotheses.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys prepared with near-perfect equimolar ratios of constituent elements.
hypotheses.boundary: There is a critical phosphorus limit beyond which excessive P may lead to the formation of crystalline or brittle P-rich phases; the beneficial effect is expected within a narrow composition window (5–10% excess).
hypotheses.uncertainty: The balance between improved network formation and the risk of phase segregation is delicate, and the precise increase in thermal stability is uncertain.

Subject both to thermal analysis using DSC and compare their crystallization onset temperatures, as well as perform XRD/TEM to assess amorphous character.
measurements: DSC for glass transition and crystallization temperatures
XRD/SAED for phase structure
Composition analysis (ICP-MS/EDX)

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis explores a compositional adjustment—increasing phosphorus content slightly beyond equimolarity—to leverage its natural affinity for forming interconnected amorphous networks, a route not investigated in the paper.

beyond_paper.reason: The proposed intervention introduces a new element (boron) and a phosphorus‐rich alloy system that is not explored or mentioned in the paper, making it an extension beyond the reported work.

paper_did: Developed a nanodroplet‐mediated electrodeposition method in which metal salt precursors are confined to water nanodroplets in an oil (dichloroethane) phase and delivered to a biased electrode for rapid (≈100 ms) reduction.

Synthesized high‐entropy metallic glass nanoparticles (HEMG‐NPs) containing up to eight equimolar metallic components (e.g., Co, Fe, La, Ni, Pt, among others) with precise stoichiometric control by tuning the precursor concentrations.

Characterized the as‐deposited NPs using TEM, SAED, SEM‐EDX, ICP‐MS, XRD, XPS, and electrochemical methods (CV, EIS) to confirm the disordered amorphous microstructure and evaluate the electrocatalytic activity.
Demonstrated multifunctional electrocatalytic performance for water splitting (both the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) and oxygen evolution reaction (OER)) with the HEMG‐NP electrocatalyst.
paper_reported: Successful electrosynthesis of amorphous HEMG‐NPs with near‐complete reduction of confined metal salt precursors and excellent stoichiometric precision (variability within 2–5%).
Confirmation of a disordered, amorphous (metallic glass) structure via diffuse SAED rings, high‐resolution TEM/HAADF‐STEM, and supporting XRD data.
Synergistic electrocatalytic performance in water electrolysis, where a CoFeLaNiPt HEMG‐NP catalyst exhibited improved OER and HER overpotentials relative to unary metal systems.

Quantitative evaluation of electrocatalytic parameters (e.g., double layer capacitance, ECSA, mass activity, Tafel slopes) demonstrating that the nanodroplet‐mediated method can yield catalysts with enhanced performance.
paper_proposed: Exploring compositional tuning by varying metal salt species and their ratios to further optimize both the electrocatalytic activity and the material properties of HEMG‐NPs.
Investigating the in situ oxidation states and catalytic mechanisms under operational conditions (e.g., using surface-interrogation scanning electrochemical microscopy).
Leveraging the versatility of the nanodroplet‐electrodeposition platform as a generalized method to design multi‐functional electrocatalysts for a wide range of reactions.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Introducing a minor silicon addition into the precursor solution for phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys will promote formation of a silicate–phosphate network that enhances glass‐forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloy synthesized via nanodroplet‐mediated electrodeposition, yielding an initially amorphous metallic glass.
hypotheses.intervention: Incorporate a small amount (e.g., 3–7 atomic %) of a silicon precursor (such as a soluble silicate or SiCl4 converted to a compatible aqueous salt) into the metal salt solution prior to emulsion preparation.
hypotheses.conditions: The silicon precursor must co‐deposit uniformly with the other metal ions and phosphorus under the existing room‐temperature, rapid electrodeposition conditions; excessive silicon may induce phase separation or formation of silicate crystals.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The added silicon promotes local formation of Si–O–P or Si–O–metal bonding motifs that integrate into the amorphous structure, increasing the network connectivity and the number of topological constraints.
hypotheses.mechanism: Silicon is a well‐known glass former; when incorporated into a phosphorus‐rich environment it can establish a rigid and interconnected network. This added connectivity reduces atomic mobility during cooling, delays nucleation events, and raises the crystallization temperature, thereby enhancing both glass‐forming ability and thermal stability.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline alloy without silicon, the silicon‐doped alloy should display a measurable increase (on the order of tens of degrees Celsius) in the onset temperature of crystallization and an extended thermal window for the amorphous phase.
hypotheses.baseline: Phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys produced by nanodroplet‐mediated electrodeposition without silicon addition.
hypotheses.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within an optimal silicon concentration window (approximately 3–7 at.%). Beyond this range the formation of secondary silicate phases may occur, counteracting the amorphous stabilization.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While qualitative improvement is expected based on known glass‐forming principles, the precise quantitative increase in thermal stability and the optimal silicon amount require experimental optimization.

hypotheses.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces silicon as a novel dopant in phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys to induce a silicate–phosphate network, a compositional strategy not explored in the paper, targeting improved glass formation and thermal stability.

hypotheses.hypothesis: A single post‐deposition ultrafast laser flash treatment applied to phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys can induce transient localized melting and rapid quenching that further suppresses nucleation and enhances the stability of the amorphous state.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: An as‐deposited, amorphous phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy produced by nanodroplet‐mediated electrodeposition.
hypotheses.intervention: Immediately after electrodeposition, subject the alloy film to a controlled, ultrafast laser pulse (in the nanosecond to microsecond range) with energy calibrated to induce surface melting of a thin layer without causing significant elemental segregation.
hypotheses.conditions: The laser fluence must be precisely set so that only a superficial re‐melt occurs and subsequent quenching is rapid enough to avoid crystallization; the treatment should be compatible with the substrate and not induce thermal damage.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: The laser pulse generates localized, transient melt‐zones that, upon rapid quenching, eliminate incipient nucleation sites and reinforce the amorphous structure by effectively “resetting” the atomic configuration.
hypotheses.mechanism: By providing a brief, high‐temperature pulse followed by ultra‐rapid cooling, any minute crystalline seeds that may have begun forming during deposition are eradicated. This additional quenching step increases the effective cooling rate beyond the intrinsic electrodeposition rate, leading to a more deeply frozen disordered state with enhanced thermal stability.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The laser‐treated samples should demonstrate a higher crystallization onset temperature and exhibit a more homogenous amorphous structure (as determined by TEM/SAED and DSC), compared to untreated controls.
hypotheses.baseline: Phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys produced by nanodroplet‐mediated electrodeposition and left without any post‐treatment.
hypotheses.boundary: The effective outcome is contingent on tuning the laser energy; if the energy is too low the intervention is ineffective, whereas excessive energy could provoke local crystallization or damage the film.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise improvement (e.g., in degrees Celsius increase in crystallization temperature) depends on optimizing the laser parameters, and the optimal window for treatment energy is uncertain without preliminary calibration.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Altering the electrodeposition protocol to a tailored pulsed potential mode will create periodic cooling intervals during the deposition of phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys, thereby reducing atomic diffusion and nucleation, which improves glass‐forming ability and enhances thermal stability.

paper_did: Synthesized MnCrFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) ribbons via melt spinning at varying wheel speeds (10, 15, 20, and 25 m/s).

Characterized the microstructure using X‐ray diffraction (XRD), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) to evaluate phase, grain size, twin boundaries, texture, and compositional homogeneity.

Evaluated mechanical properties through microhardness testing and uniaxial tensile tests to correlate processing parameters (wheel speed and ribbon thickness) with strength, ductility, and fracture modes.
paper_reported: The HEA ribbons consistently exhibit a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) structure with refined, equiaxed grains (average sizes around 4.8 μm at 10 m/s and 3.3 μm at 25 m/s) and a noticeable presence of Σ3 twin boundaries (approximately 7.36% at 10 m/s).

Mechanical testing revealed that slower wheel speeds (e.g., 10 m/s) yield thicker ribbons with a balanced combination of enhanced strength (≈300 MPa) and ductility (up to 8% elongation), whereas higher speeds (25 m/s) resulted in brittle behavior (≈35 MPa tensile strength) likely due to inhomogeneities and defects.

Cooling rate differences between the cooling surface (contact with the Cu wheel) and the free surface induce texture variations and affect overall mechanical response, with increased hardness attributed dominantly to the grain size refinement achieved during rapid solidification.
paper_proposed: Using melt spinning with controlled wheel speeds as a processing route to tailor microstructure and mechanical properties of HEA ribbons, with a suggestion that these ribbons could be further processed (e.g., crushed into powders) to extend their application scope.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Introduce a minor alloying addition of zirconium (Zr) into the phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy to form strong Zr–P short-range bonds that help suppress crystallization.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced by rapid solidification that exhibits marginal glass-forming ability and limited thermal stability in its amorphous state.
hypotheses.intervention: Add a small concentration (e.g., 1–5 at.%) of zirconium into the alloy formulation.
hypotheses.conditions: The alloy is rapidly solidified (e.g., via melt spinning) and the Zr content is maintained below the threshold where separate Zr-phosphide crystalline phases would form; effective in cooling regimes where limited time is available for atomic rearrangements.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of localized Zr–P clusters or chemical short-range order within the amorphous matrix.
hypotheses.mechanism: Zr has a strong chemical affinity for phosphorus, and its incorporation can lead to the formation of stable, localized bonds that increase the nucleation barrier for crystallization. The formation of such Zr–P clusters can also hinder atomic mobility, thereby improving thermal stability of the glassy state by retarding devitrification.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: An increased glass-forming ability that allows formation of a fully amorphous structure under slightly slower cooling rates and an elevated crystallization (devitrification) temperature by, potentially, tens of degrees over the baseline alloy.
hypotheses.baseline: The corresponding alloy without Zr addition, which shows lower glass-forming ability and earlier onset of crystallization upon heating.
hypotheses.boundary: The intervention is expected to work only in a limited composition window; excessive Zr may lead to separate Zr-phosphide crystalline phases, adversely affecting both glass forming and thermal stability.
hypotheses.uncertainty: Quantitative improvement levels (e.g., exact temperature shifts) are moderately uncertain and need experimental verification.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Implement a controlled sub–glass-transition (sub‐Tg) annealing treatment immediately after rapid quenching to relax internal stresses and reduce free volume, thereby enhancing both glass-forming ability and thermal stability.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced as a rapidly quenched amorphous ribbon with residual internal stresses and excess free volume that predisposes it to premature crystallization.
hypotheses.intervention: Apply a short, isothermal annealing treatment at a temperature slightly below the glass transition temperature (Tg) for a controlled period.
hypotheses.conditions: Annealing temperature should be selected to be just under Tg (e.g., Tg − 20°C to Tg − 50°C) and the dwell time optimized (from minutes to an hour) to allow stress relaxation without triggering crystallization.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Reduction of free volume and annihilation of residual stresses within the amorphous matrix, leading to a denser, relaxed structure.
hypotheses.mechanism: By annealing at sub–Tg temperatures, the alloy undergoes structural relaxation where free volume is reduced. This relaxation increases the kinetic barrier to nucleation and diminishes the driving force for crystallization, thereby extending the thermal stability range of the amorphous state.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is anticipated to exhibit an increased crystallization temperature (Tx) and improved resistance to thermal devitrification, with possibly a moderate increase in Tg, compared to the as-quenched state.
hypotheses.baseline: The as-quenched alloy without any post-solidification annealing, which retains higher free volume and internal stresses, leading to lower thermal stability.
hypotheses.boundary: The effectiveness is contingent on precise control of the annealing temperature and time; exceeding the optimal range may induce partial crystallization.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the thermal stabilization effect is uncertain and will depend on the optimization of the annealing parameters.

hypotheses.hypothesis: Utilize a controlled mild surface oxidation treatment post–rapid solidification to form an ultra-thin, stable oxide layer that inhibits heterogeneous nucleation and retards crystallization in the amorphous alloy.
hypotheses.material_initial_state: A rapidly solidified, phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy in the amorphous state that is subject to premature surface-initiated crystallization.
hypotheses.intervention: Expose the freshly prepared amorphous alloy ribbons to a controlled, low-oxygen partial pressure environment to induce the formation of a thin, uniform oxide layer on the surface.
hypotheses.conditions: The oxidation should be mild, conducted at low temperatures (well below Tg) and for short durations to form a nanometer-scale oxide without compromising the bulk amorphous structure.
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-thin surface oxide that acts as a barrier to heterogeneous nucleation, thereby reducing the propagation of crystallization from the surface inward.
hypotheses.mechanism: A controlled surface oxide layer can serve as a kinetic barrier for atomic rearrangements by passivating reactive sites and reducing surface free energy, which in turn delays the onset of crystallization. This enhances the overall thermal stability of the amorphous state by mitigating surface-mediated devitrification pathways.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The treated samples are expected to show a higher onset temperature for crystallization (Tx) in DSC measurements relative to untreated samples, with no signs of deleterious phase formation from over-oxidation.
hypotheses.baseline: Amorphous alloys without the surface oxidation treatment, which are more susceptible to heterogeneous nucleation and earlier crystallization upon heating.
hypotheses.boundary: The oxidation treatment must be precisely controlled; too strong or prolonged oxidation may lead to the growth of a thick oxide layer that could adversely affect the alloy’s properties.
hypotheses.uncertainty: While the mechanism is plausible, the exact degree of improvement in thermal stability is uncertain and depends on the control over oxide layer thickness and uniformity.

pool.label: C1
pool.builds_on: The paper’s demonstration that cooling rate significantly influences amorphization and phase transformations, combined with principles of controlled thermal relaxation in amorphous solids.
pool.what_is_new: Proposes a novel processing route—a tailored two-stage cooling profile—to achieve a more stable amorphous state, offering a different mechanism from solely compositional or post-processing interventions discussed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Implementing a two-stage cooling protocol—starting with an ultra-rapid quench from the melt followed by a controlled moderate cooling phase—will enhance both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing HEAs.
fields.material_initial_state: The molten state of a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy similar to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 prior to quenching.
fields.intervention: Adopt a dual-stage cooling method: first, apply an ultra-high cooling rate (≥10⁵ K/s) to 'freeze in' the disordered atomic structure, then switch to a moderate cooling rate (≈10³ K/s) once below the liquid state but above ambient, allowing controlled structural relaxation.
fields.conditions: Requires precise control of the cooling profile using advanced quenching equipment; the transition temperature between the ultra-rapid and moderate cooling stages must be optimized to avoid premature crystallization.
fields.structural_mediator: A balanced amorphous structure with reduced residual stresses and free volume thanks to controlled relaxation, while maintaining a fully amorphous state.
fields.mechanism: The ultra-rapid quench initially suppresses nucleation and crystalline growth, ensuring the formation of an amorphous structure. The subsequent moderate cooling stage allows gradual atomic rearrangements that relieve internal stresses and stabilize the amorphous configuration without crossing crystallization thresholds.
fields.predicted_outcome: Amorphous alloys produced via the two-stage cooling protocol will display higher crystallization onset temperatures in DSC measurements and improved homogeneity (as verified by XRD and TEM), compared to those produced by a constant ultra-rapid quench.
fields.baseline: Samples produced by conventional melt-spinning that apply a constant ultra-rapid cooling rate throughout.
fields.boundary: This approach is effective only if the moderate cooling phase is sufficiently fast to avoid unwanted crystallization yet slow enough to allow controlled relaxation; mis-tuning can result in partial crystallization.
fields.uncertainty: Precisely determining the optimum transition temperature and cooling rates requires iterative experimentation; the magnitude of the improvement is not precisely predictable a priori.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of amorphous alloy samples: one using standard constant ultra-rapid melt-spinning and one using the two-stage cooling protocol. Use DSC to determine crystallization onset temperatures and employ XRD/TEM to assess amorphous structure quality.
measurements: DSC curves comparing crystallization onset temperatures
XRD diffraction patterns to confirm amorphous structure
TEM micrographs for structural homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the two-stage cooled samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in thermal stability (e.g., higher crystallization onset temperature) and better amorphous homogeneity relative to the constant quenching baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C2
pool.builds_on: The concept that processing conditions, particularly high-pressure quenching, can enhance glass formation by suppressing atomic diffusion—a mechanism also relevant in the formation of biological glasses.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the idea of pressure-assisted stabilization of amorphous structures to phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys, proposing a novel processing route rather than a compositional modification.

fields.hypothesis: Applying high-pressure conditions during rapid solidification of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys improves glass-forming ability and thermal stability by reducing atomic mobility and enhancing viscous undercooling.
fields.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced via conventional rapid quenching under ambient pressure.
fields.intervention: Introduce a high-pressure quenching step (e.g., applying several gigapascals during solidification) in the processing route.
fields.conditions: The intervention is effective when high pressure is maintained during the melt-to-amorphous transformation; the alloy composition must tolerate the applied pressure without triggering pressure-induced phase transformations not related to amorphization.
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced viscous undercooling caused by pressure-induced densification which suppresses atomic diffusion.
fields.mechanism: High pressure during quenching increases the viscosity of the melt and reduces atomic mobility, thereby delaying or inhibiting nucleation and growth of crystalline phases. This increased resistance to atomic rearrangement promotes the formation and stabilization of an amorphous structure, ultimately improving the alloy’s glass-forming ability and thermal stability.
fields.predicted_outcome: The high-pressure quenched samples are expected to exhibit a lowered crystallization rate, increased glass transition temperatures, and overall enhanced thermal stability compared to samples quenched at ambient pressure.
fields.baseline: Phosphorus-containing alloy processed under conventional ambient-pressure rapid quenching.
fields.boundary: This approach is effective only if the applied pressure is high enough to influence viscosity without inducing alternative high-pressure phases; excessive pressure may lead to undesired structural changes.
fields.uncertainty: The optimum pressure range and the exact magnitude of improvement in glass-forming ability remain to be determined through systematic study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples; process one set under ambient pressure and another set under controlled high-pressure conditions during rapid quenching.
measurements: DSC to measure glass transition and crystallization temperatures.
XRD to confirm amorphous versus crystalline content.
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess local structural differences.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-pressure quenched samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in glass transition temperature or show similar crystallization behavior compared to ambient-pressure samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C3
pool.builds_on: The paper’s examination of kinetic stabilization and critical cooling rates, extended here by employing a post-production thermal treatment to relax the amorphous structure and further impede devitrification.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a single post-solidification thermal intervention—sub‐Tg annealing—to enhance the thermal stability of phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy glasses, a strategy that departs from compositional or high-pressure interventions discussed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A controlled sub‐glass-transition (sub‐Tg) annealing treatment applied to as-cast phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy amorphous alloys will enhance their thermal stability and reduce the propensity for crystallization.
fields.material_initial_state: An as-cast phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy or compositionally complex alloy that has been successfully vitrified using conventional rapid solidification techniques.
fields.intervention: Subject the as-cast amorphous alloy to a post-production annealing treatment at a temperature slightly below the glass transition temperature (approximately Tg − 20 K) for a predetermined duration (e.g., several hours) under an inert atmosphere.
fields.conditions: The annealing temperature must be controlled to remain below Tg, ensuring that the material undergoes structural relaxation without initiating crystallization. The dwell time should be optimized; too long may initiate unwanted crystallization, while too short may not allow sufficient relaxation.
fields.structural_mediator: Sub-Tg annealing facilitates atomic rearrangements that reduce excess free volume and internal stresses, leading to a more uniform and tightly packed amorphous structure.
fields.mechanism: The thermal treatment at sub-Tg promotes structural relaxation in the amorphous state, which reduces local energy inhomogeneities and minimizes heterogeneous nucleation sites for crystallization. This in turn increases the effective energy barrier for crystallization and raises the thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
fields.predicted_outcome: The annealed alloy is expected to exhibit a higher crystallization onset temperature in DSC measurements (indicative of improved thermal stability) and a more homogeneous microstructure compared to the as-cast baseline. While this post-formation treatment may not affect the glass-forming ability per se, it should enhance the resistance to devitrification during subsequent thermal cycling.
fields.baseline: The same alloy in its as-cast, unannealed state.
fields.boundary: Annealing temperatures too close to or above Tg might trigger partial or full crystallization; the treatment must be optimized to ensure only relaxation is achieved.
fields.uncertainty: Although sub‐Tg annealing is known to improve thermal stability in metallic glasses generally, the precise quantitative enhancement for phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys remains uncertain and may depend on the specific alloy composition and annealing schedule.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the amorphous alloy: one set is kept as-cast (baseline) and the other is subjected to a controlled sub‐Tg annealing treatment (e.g., at Tg − 20 K for several hours) under inert atmosphere.
measurements: DSC analysis to determine and compare the crystallization onset temperatures and supercooled liquid region widths.
Microscopic structural analysis (e.g., TEM or SEM) to assess the homogeneity of the amorphous structure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a reproducible and statistically significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature or improved microstructural homogeneity compared to the as-cast samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C4
pool.builds_on: The concept from the paper that increasing atomic size disparity (as captured by the δ′ parameter) can be achieved via similar element substitution to control the amorphous phase.
pool.what_is_new: This approach tests the introduction of a rare-earth element (cerium) to modulate lattice distortion in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys—a strategy that extends the principles outlined in the paper to a different class of dopants and alloy systems.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporating a small amount of cerium (approximately 1–3 at.%) into phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys will improve glass-forming ability and thermal stability by increasing the overall atomic size disparity and lattice distortion.
fields.material_initial_state: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys with a balanced mix of refractory and transition metals making up a moderate range of atomic sizes.
fields.intervention: Substitute 1–3 at.% of one of the larger metallic components with cerium, ensuring homogeneous distribution in the melt.
fields.conditions: The intervention is expected to be effective under rapid solidification conditions where cerium can uniformly participate in the alloy matrix; if cerium segregates or if cooling rates are too slow, the benefits may not be realized.
fields.structural_mediator: An increased atomic size mismatch that raises the δ′ parameter, leading to enhanced lattice distortion and a more deeply metastable amorphous structure.
fields.mechanism: Cerium has a comparatively large atomic radius relative to typical transition metals in such alloys. Its substitution increases atomic size disparity, which in turn elevates the lattice distortion, hindering the mobility necessary for crystallization during cooling. This increases both the glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
fields.predicted_outcome: An observable widening of the supercooled liquid region along with an increase in the maximum critical casting diameter compared to alloys without cerium, indicating improved resistance to crystallization.
fields.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys without cerium addition that demonstrate comparatively lower values of δ′ and more readily crystallize.
fields.boundary: The effectiveness is limited to low cerium concentrations; high levels might provoke phase separation or induce deleterious intermetallic compounds due to solubility limits.
fields.uncertainty: While the expected mechanistic benefits are supported by principles of atomic size mismatch, the quantitative improvement in glass stability remains to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy samples with 0%, 1%, and 3% cerium substitution under identical casting conditions. Use DSC to measure the supercooled liquid region and determine the critical casting diameter via XRD structural analysis.
measurements: DSC curves to assess Tg, Tx, and ΔT
Critical casting diameter measurements
XRD analysis to confirm amorphous structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the cerium-containing samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the supercooled liquid region or critical casting thickness compared to the no-cerium baseline, or if they exhibit signs of enhanced crystallinity, the hypothesis is falsified.

fields.material_initial_state: A fully amorphous phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced by conventional arc melting and rapid melt spinning, characterized by high configurational entropy and a disordered metallic bonding environment.
fields.intervention: Incorporate 1–2 at.% yttrium into the precursor mix prior to melting, ensuring complete dissolution and homogeneous distribution.
fields.conditions: The Y content must be maintained in the 1–2 at.% range to avoid forming Y‑rich intermetallic phases; processing requires careful control of melting and cooling conditions under an inert atmosphere.
fields.structural_mediator: Y atoms, due to their significantly larger atomic radius compared to the other constituent elements, create local atomic size mismatches that increase packing frustration and hinder the nucleation of crystalline phases.
fields.mechanism: Unlike localized covalent bonding, in metallic glasses the dominant bonding is delocalized. The introduction of Y increases the excess configurational entropy via atomic size mismatch. This enhanced mismatch disrupts the regular packing, thereby raising the free energy barrier for crystallization, leading to an extended supercooled liquid region and improved thermal stability.
fields.predicted_outcome: DSC scans are expected to show a broader supercooled liquid region and a higher or more distinctly observed glass transition (Tg). fields.baseline: The phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy synthesized without any yttrium addition, under identical processing conditions.
fields.boundary: If the Y content exceeds ~2 at.%, there is a risk of forming Y‑rich intermetallic compounds that could deteriorate the amorphous character; conversely, if below 1 at.%, the atomic size mismatch may be insufficient to impact nucleation kinetics.
fields.uncertainty: While atomic size mismatch is a recognized mechanism for enhancing glass-forming ability, the exact quantitative improvement in the supercooled liquid region width or thermal stability is uncertain without further systematic studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one series with 1–2 at.% Y added and one series of the baseline alloy without Y. Use identical arc melting and melt-spinning procedures under inert atmosphere with multiple remelting cycles for homogeneity.

X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the continued amorphous structure and absence of Y‑rich intermetallic phases.
Nanoindentation or dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) to measure any changes in mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y‑doped samples do not show a statistically significant extension of the supercooled liquid region, an upward shift or sharpening of the glass transition, or present any detectable Y‑rich crystalline phases compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

fields.material_initial_state: A molten phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy prepared for rapid quenching.
fields.intervention: Integrate an in situ acoustic vibration system that applies controlled, low-amplitude ultrasound (or high-frequency acoustic waves) during the quenching process, where the optimal frequency and amplitude are pre-determined by simulation to ensure atomic-scale perturbations without inducing cavitation or unwanted nucleation.
fields.conditions: The acoustic parameters (frequency, amplitude, and duration) must be calibrated through detailed simulation studies and sensitivity analyses such that the energy input remains within the linear response regime of the material, affecting only localized regions at the advancing solid–liquid interface during the entire rapid solidification window.
fields.structural_mediator: An acoustically perturbed SRO state featuring enhanced chemical disorder at the interface, which reduces the formation of nucleation-favorable atomic clusters and increases the barrier to crystallization.
fields.mechanism: The applied acoustic vibrations serve as an external athermal mixing mechanism analogous to the athermal events described in the paper, which disrupt the inherent self-organizing tendencies of atoms at the solid–liquid interface. This results in a frozen SRO configuration that is more disordered, thereby enhancing the kinetic barrier against crystallization. Simulation-based calibration ensures that the vibrations are strong enough to perturb atomic order without causing adverse effects like cavitation or accelerating diffusion.
fields.predicted_outcome: Alloy samples processed with acoustic vibrations during quenching are expected to show (i) broader and more diffuse XRD scattering profiles, (ii) an elevated crystallization onset temperature in DSC measurements, and (iii) local SRO metrics indicating increased disorder compared to samples quenched without acoustic intervention.
fields.baseline: Identical alloy samples rapidly solidified without the application of acoustic vibrations.
fields.boundary: If the vibration amplitude or frequency falls outside the calibrated optimal range, the intervention may either be too weak to affect SRO or too strong, triggering unwanted nucleation events or cavitation effects. Its success is contingent upon maintaining finely tuned vibrational parameters.
fields.uncertainty: The precise vibrational parameters (frequency and amplitude) that yield the desired modification in SRO without adverse effects remain to be accurately determined via comprehensive simulation and preliminary experimental studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one processed with the calibrated acoustic vibrations during rapid quenching and one without. Analyze both groups using XRD to evaluate amorphous scattering profiles, DSC to measure crystallization onset temperatures, and local structural probes (e.g., pair distribution function analysis or atom probe tomography) to quantify SRO.
measurements: XRD profiles for amorphous vs. crystalline features
DSC crystallization onset temperature
Local SRO characterization metrics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vibrated samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in terms of increased amorphous stability or alterations in local SRO relative to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C11
pool.builds_on: The rapid electro-shock synthesis method described in the paper, which relies on fast quenching to achieve amorphous microstructures, is extended by adding a subsequent laser-induced quenching step.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes the novel use of an ultrafast laser flash treatment post electrodeposition as a processing intervention to further kinetically trap the amorphous state in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys—a strategy not addressed in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: A single post‐deposition ultrafast laser flash treatment applied to phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys can induce transient localized melting and rapid quenching that further suppresses nucleation and enhances the stability of the amorphous state.
fields.material_initial_state: An as‐deposited, amorphous phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy produced by nanodroplet‐mediated electrodeposition.
fields.intervention: Immediately after electrodeposition, subject the alloy film to a controlled, ultrafast laser pulse (in the nanosecond to microsecond range) with energy calibrated to induce surface melting of a thin layer without causing significant elemental segregation.
fields.conditions: The laser fluence must be precisely set so that only a superficial re‐melt occurs and subsequent quenching is rapid enough to avoid crystallization; the treatment should be compatible with the substrate and not induce thermal damage.
fields.structural_mediator: The laser pulse generates localized, transient melt‐zones that, upon rapid quenching, eliminate incipient nucleation sites and reinforce the amorphous structure by effectively “resetting” the atomic configuration.
fields.mechanism: By providing a brief, high‐temperature pulse followed by ultra‐rapid cooling, any minute crystalline seeds that may have begun forming during deposition are eradicated. This additional quenching step increases the effective cooling rate beyond the intrinsic electrodeposition rate, leading to a more deeply frozen disordered state with enhanced thermal stability.
fields.predicted_outcome: The laser‐treated samples should demonstrate a higher crystallization onset temperature and exhibit a more homogenous amorphous structure (as determined by TEM/SAED and DSC), compared to untreated controls.
fields.baseline: Phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys produced by nanodroplet‐mediated electrodeposition and left without any post‐treatment.
fields.boundary: The effective outcome is contingent on tuning the laser energy; if the energy is too low the intervention is ineffective, whereas excessive energy could provoke local crystallization or damage the film.
fields.uncertainty: The precise improvement (e.g., in degrees Celsius increase in crystallization temperature) depends on optimizing the laser parameters, and the optimal window for treatment energy is uncertain without preliminary calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Divide as‐deposited phosphorus‐containing alloy films into two groups. Subject one group to the specified ultrafast laser pulse treatment while leaving the other as a control. Use DSC to measure crystallization and glass transition temperatures and employ TEM/SAED to analyze the microstructure. Compare the thermal stability and amorphous quality between the two groups.
measurements: DSC to determine the crystallization onset and glass transition temperatures
TEM/SAED to assess amorphous versus crystalline structure
Surface morphology analysis (e.g., AFM) to check for laser‐induced damage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the laser‐treated samples do not show a statistically significant increase in the crystallization onset temperature or if they exhibit evidence of crystallization/damage compared to the control, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C12
pool.builds_on: the principle that improved atomic size mismatch can enhance glass formation by frustrating crystallization, a concept well established in metallic glass science.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis specifically applies minor zirconium microalloying in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys to promote kinetic stabilization of the amorphous state, a strategy not reported in the referenced paper.

fields.hypothesis: Small additions of zirconium will improve the glass‐forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy.
fields.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing compositionally complex alloy formulated to be near the threshold of glass formation via rapid quenching but that tends to crystallize under conventional processing.
fields.intervention: Introduce a minor addition (e.g., 2–5 at.%) of zirconium into the alloy during initial synthesis.
fields.conditions: The zirconium content must be precisely controlled to avoid forming separate intermetallic phases, and the alloy should be rapidly quenched in an inert atmosphere.
fields.structural_mediator: Enhanced local atomic mismatch and packing frustration resulting from the large atomic size difference introduced by zirconium.
fields.mechanism: Zirconium, with its large atomic radius relative to the other constituent elements and its high affinity for mixing, can increase the topological and chemical complexity. This increased mismatch and frustrated packing raise the critical cooling rate required for nucleation and crystallization, thereby promoting a more robust amorphous structure and enhancing its thermal stability (manifested as a higher crystallization onset temperature, Tx).
fields.predicted_outcome: A lower critical cooling rate for full amorphization and a higher Tx by an expected margin of tens of degrees Celsius compared to the baseline phosphorus-containing alloy without zirconium.
fields.baseline: The analogous phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy without any zirconium addition, which exhibits only marginal amorphous formation and relatively lower Tx.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is anticipated only within a narrow zirconium addition range; excessive Zr may lead to the formation of unwanted intermetallic phases that could detract from the amorphous stability.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement in glass-forming ability and Tx is uncertain and will require calibration of the zirconium concentration.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys with 0, 2, 3.5, and 5 at.% zirconium. Process all samples by rapid quenching in an inert atmosphere. Characterize the samples via XRD to quantify the amorphous versus crystalline content and DSC to measure the crystallization onset temperature (Tx).
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase analysis
Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine Tx and glass transition temperature (Tg)
Microscopy (e.g., TEM) to assess nanoscale structural homogeneity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the zirconium-doped samples do not exhibit a significant increase in the amorphous phase fraction or a higher Tx relative to the zirconium-free baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

pool.label: C13
pool.builds_on: the established concept in glass science that network formers like silicon can bond with phosphorus to create stable, interconnected structures, drawing analogies from phosphosilicate glasses.
pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis uniquely proposes using controlled silicon microalloying to induce in situ formation of P–Si networks in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys, thereby enhancing their glass-forming ability and thermal stability—a concept not addressed in the referenced paper.

fields.hypothesis: Minor silicon addition will promote the in situ formation of P–Si network motifs, thereby enhancing the glass‐forming ability and thermal stability of the amorphous phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy.
fields.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing compositionally complex alloy that, under rapid solidification, exhibits insufficient network connectivity and marginal glass formation.
fields.intervention: Add a small amount (e.g., 2–4 at.%) of silicon during alloy melting.
fields.conditions: The silicon content must remain low enough to avoid the formation of silicide precipitates and should be processed by rapid solidification in an inert atmosphere.
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of short-range P–Si bonds that act similarly to the network structures found in phosphosilicate glasses.
fields.mechanism: Silicon, as a metalloid with a strong tendency to form covalent bonds with phosphorus, will bond preferentially to phosphorus atoms in the melt. This interaction leads to the formation of P–Si network motifs that increase the viscosity and chemical homogeneity of the undercooled liquid, thus raising the kinetic barrier against crystallization. The resulting amorphous structure should display an enhanced crystallization onset temperature and improved overall thermal stability.
fields.predicted_outcome: A lower critical cooling rate for achieving a fully amorphous state and an increase in the crystallization onset temperature (Tx) by an amount on the order of several tens of degrees Celsius relative to the silicon-free alloy.
fields.baseline: The analogous phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy prepared without silicon, which suffers from limited network formation and a lower thermal stability of the amorphous state.
fields.boundary: Improvement is expected only within a narrow silicon composition range; higher silicon levels risk forming crystalline silicide phases that could undermine the amorphous stability.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal silicon concentration and the precise quantitative improvement in Tx remain uncertain and must be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys with varying silicon additions (e.g., 0, 2, 3, and 4 at.%). Process all compositions using rapid quenching in an inert atmosphere. Characterize the samples using XRD to assess the amorphous content, DSC to measure Tg and Tx, and spectroscopic techniques (e.g., XPS) to detect the presence of P–Si bonds.
measurements: XRD to verify the degree of amorphization
DSC to determine the glass transition and crystallization temperatures
XPS or similar spectroscopy to confirm P–Si network formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the silicon-doped samples do not exhibit a higher amorphous phase fraction or an elevated Tx (and no evidence for P–Si bond formation is detected) compared to the silicon-free control, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C6
top3.builds_on: The paper establishes that high‑entropy effects can substantially alter the atomic energy landscape in metallic glasses (PMC9023469::web::017). This hypothesis builds on that by using a minor compositional tweak (Hf addition) to further manipulate the free energy landscape through enhanced mixing enthalpy and atomic size mismatch.
top3.what_is_new: This approach introduces Hf as a dopant in phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloys, capitalizing on its intrinsic properties to further hinder crystallization—a strategy distinct from the bonding motifs proposed in other dopant scenarios and not addressed in the original study.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor amount (1–3 at.%) of hafnium (Hf) into a phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy will improve its glass‑forming ability and thermal stability by leveraging Hf’s strong negative mixing enthalpy and substantial atomic size to further disrupt crystallization.
fields.material_initial_state: An amorphous phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced by conventional arc melting and rapid quenching, characterized by high configurational disorder and a metallic bonding network.
fields.intervention: Add 1–3 at.% hafnium to the alloy’s composition prior to melting, ensuring thorough mixing and homogeneity during arc melting and subsequent rapid solidification.
fields.conditions: The Hf content should remain within 1–3 at.% so as to avoid phase separation or the formation of Hf‑rich intermetallic compounds; processing must be done under inert atmosphere with sufficient remelting steps to guarantee uniform distribution.
fields.structural_mediator: Hafnium, with its large atomic radius and a strong negative heat of mixing with transition metals, introduces local chemical heterogeneity and enhances atomic size mismatch, thus increasing the overall excess configurational entropy.
fields.mechanism: The presence of Hf in the alloy disrupts regular atomic packing by inducing local compositional fluctuations. Its strong chemical affinity with other metallic constituents and sizable atomic size elevate the free energy barrier for crystallization. This thermodynamic penalty for nucleation helps to extend the stability of the amorphous state by suppressing crystallization kinetics.
fields.predicted_outcome: DSC analysis should show an extended supercooled liquid region and an upward shift in the crystallization onset temperature relative to the baseline alloy. XRD and TEM should confirm the retention of an entirely amorphous structure, and mechanical testing (e.g., nanoindentation) may reveal enhanced hardness or modulus due to a more stabilized short-range order.
fields.baseline: The phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy fabricated without the addition of Hf under identical processing conditions.
fields.boundary: If the Hf concentration is too high (above ~3 at.%), there is a risk of Hf segregation or the formation of Hf‑rich intermetallic phases which would negate the glass‑forming benefits.
fields.uncertainty: Although Hf’s role in increasing mixing entropy and disrupts crystallization is supported by general metallic glass principles, the precise magnitude of the effect in phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloys remains to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of alloy samples: one batch with 1–3 at.% Hf added and a control batch without Hf. Use consistent arc melting and rapid quenching protocols along with multiple remelting cycles to ensure compositional homogeneity.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to record changes in the supercooled liquid region and the onset temperature of crystallization.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the amorphous structure and rule out the presence of Hf‑rich phases.
Nanoindentation or dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) to compare any enhancements in mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Hf‑doped samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in glass‑forming ability (e.g., no extension of the supercooled liquid region or shift in crystallization onset) or if phase segregation is observed, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C5
top3.builds_on: The paper demonstrates that high‐entropy enhances the energetic and structural disorder in metallic glasses (PMC9023469::web::017). This hypothesis extends that concept by further destabilizing crystallization through increased atomic size mismatch.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a specific compositional intervention (minor Y doping) that leverages entropic and size-mismatch effects, as opposed to introducing localized directional bonds, to improve glass-forming ability and thermal stability in a metallic system.

fields.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount (1–2 at.%) of a large-atomic-radius dopant such as yttrium (Y) to a phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy will improve its glass‑forming ability and thermal stability by increasing atomic size mismatch and packing frustration without relying on directional bonding.
fields.material_initial_state: A fully amorphous phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy or compositionally complex alloy produced by conventional arc melting and rapid melt spinning, characterized by high configurational entropy and a disordered metallic bonding environment.
fields.intervention: Incorporate 1–2 at.% yttrium into the precursor mix prior to melting, ensuring complete dissolution and homogeneous distribution.
fields.conditions: The Y content must be maintained in the 1–2 at.% range to avoid forming Y‑rich intermetallic phases; processing requires careful control of melting and cooling conditions under an inert atmosphere.
fields.structural_mediator: Y atoms, due to their significantly larger atomic radius compared to the other constituent elements, create local atomic size mismatches that increase packing frustration and hinder the nucleation of crystalline phases.
fields.mechanism: Unlike localized covalent bonding, in metallic glasses the dominant bonding is delocalized. The introduction of Y increases the excess configurational entropy via atomic size mismatch. This enhanced mismatch disrupts the regular packing, thereby raising the free energy barrier for crystallization, leading to an extended supercooled liquid region and improved thermal stability.
fields.predicted_outcome: DSC scans are expected to show a broader supercooled liquid region and a higher or more distinctly observed glass transition (Tg). XRD and TEM should confirm that the amorphous structure is maintained, while nanoindentation or DMA may reveal modest improvements in hardness or elastic modulus.
fields.baseline: The phosphorus‑containing high‑entropy alloy synthesized without any yttrium addition, under identical processing conditions.
fields.boundary: If the Y content exceeds ~2 at.%, there is a risk of forming Y‑rich intermetallic compounds that could deteriorate the amorphous character; conversely, if below 1 at.%, the atomic size mismatch may be insufficient to impact nucleation kinetics.
fields.uncertainty: While atomic size mismatch is a recognized mechanism for enhancing glass-forming ability, the exact quantitative improvement in the supercooled liquid region width or thermal stability is uncertain without further systematic studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one series with 1–2 at.% Y added and one series of the baseline alloy without Y. Use identical arc melting and melt-spinning procedures under inert atmosphere with multiple remelting cycles for homogeneity.
measurements: Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to assess Tg, supercooled liquid region width, and crystallization exotherms.
X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the continued amorphous structure and absence of Y‑rich intermetallic phases.
Nanoindentation or dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) to measure any changes in mechanical properties.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y‑doped samples do not show a statistically significant extension of the supercooled liquid region, an upward shift or sharpening of the glass transition, or present any detectable Y‑rich crystalline phases compared to the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C7
top3.builds_on: the finding that high configurational entropy and sluggish diffusion enhance thermal stability and retard crystallization in metallic glasses (PMC8219663)
top3.what_is_new: Introducing a minor high-field-strength dopant (yttrium) to further tailor atomic-level diffusion and nanoscale chemical homogeneity in phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys—a strategy not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of a high-field-strength element such as yttrium (≈2 at.%) to phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys enhances their glass forming ability and thermal stability.
fields.material_initial_state: A phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy in the amorphous state (for example, Pd20Pt20Cu20Ni20P20) produced by rapid quenching.
fields.intervention: Introduce about 2 atomic percent yttrium during alloy preparation.
fields.conditions: Melt-spinning under inert atmosphere with cooling rates comparable to baseline; care must be taken to ensure that the yttrium level does not exceed the limit where phase separation or crystallization-inducing precipitates occur.
fields.structural_mediator: The yttrium atoms, due to their large atomic size and high field strength, induce additional local strain fields and enhance chemical disorder by increasing atomic size mismatch, which refines the nanoscale chemical heterogeneity.
fields.mechanism: The enhanced size mismatch and local bonding effects further hinder atomic mobility by increasing the activation energy for long-range diffusion (i.e. delaying the formation and percolation of shear transformation zones). This further depresses the α-relaxation dynamics and retards crystallization, leading to improved thermal stability of the amorphous phase.
fields.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Y-doped alloy should exhibit a higher crystallization activation energy, increased viscosity near Tg, and an improved critical casting thickness due to enhanced glass forming ability.
fields.baseline: Phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloys processed without yttrium addition.
fields.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only for low yttrium contents (typically 1–3 at.%) beyond which excessive doping may lead to undesirable phase separation or crystallization.
fields.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvement (e.g., percentage increase in crystallization activation energy) is uncertain, though a moderate improvement (<20%) is expected based on similar diffusion-suppressing effects observed in high-entropy systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys: one set of the baseline phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy and one set with 2 at.% Y added. Subject both sets to identical rapid quenching (e.g., melt spinning) and characterize them using DSC (to determine Tg and Tx), DMA (to assess α-relaxation behavior), and TMA (to measure viscosity near Tg).
measurements: DSC curves and determination of onset Tg and Tx
Activation energies from Kissinger analysis
DMA loss modulus and α-relaxation temperatures
Viscosity measurements near Tg via TMA
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Y-doped alloy shows no significant improvement (within experimental error) in glass forming ability or thermal stability (e.g., similar Tg, Tx, and activation energies compared to the baseline), the hypothesis is falsified.
